# Self-hosting AI models: A guide to privacy, control, and costs

## TL;DR: How do you self-host AI models?

To self-host an AI model, obtain model weights you are licensed to use, run them with a compatible inference runtime, and operate the compute, storage, and endpoint your application needs. You can use local hardware, rented GPU infrastructure, or a managed deployment platform.

- Choose the model for the task: Evaluate response quality, licence terms, memory requirements, and runtime support before selecting hardware.
- Size the whole workload: Model weights, context length, concurrent requests, and runtime overhead all affect memory consumption.
- Protect the serving endpoint: Configure authentication, network access, secrets, and logging before sending sensitive data.
- Measure the economics: Include idle capacity, storage, supporting compute, and engineering time when comparing self-hosting with a model API.
- Use managed GPU deployment where it helps: Northflank runs model-serving containers and GPU jobs on its managed cloud or customer infrastructure.

Run your model in an environment you can configure and scale. Get started with Northflank, or request GPU capacity for your workload.

Self-hosting AI models gives you control over the model version, serving software, and infrastructure used for inference. For teams building AI applications, that can make customisation, private networking, and capacity planning easier to align with the product.

It also gives you operational responsibilities. Someone must keep the endpoint available, manage model updates, protect data, and pay for capacity between requests. This guide explains when that trade makes sense and how to deploy a model without confusing infrastructure control with automatic privacy or cost savings.

## What does self-hosting an AI model mean?

Self-hosting an AI model means operating the software that loads its weights and generates predictions, instead of calling a provider's managed model endpoint.

You do not have to own the physical server. A model running in a rented GPU container is still self-hosted at the model-serving layer if you control the weights, runtime, configuration, and deployment. A managed platform can operate the infrastructure underneath it.

This is also different from running a coding agent in your own workspace. Hosting Claude Code or Codex CLI changes where its tools execute; it does not give you the proprietary model weights behind the agent. The agent may still send requests to an external model provider.

## When should you self-host AI models?

Self-hosting is useful when control over the model, deployment boundary, or serving behaviour justifies the operational work.

| Requirement | How self-hosting can help | What you still need to manage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Private inference | Place model execution near private applications and data | Network access, logging, backups, and external dependencies |
| Model customisation | Select weights, adapters, quantisation, and runtime settings | Licence compliance, compatibility, and quality evaluation |
| Predictable sustained demand | Allocate capacity around measured throughput | Utilisation, scaling, failures, and spare capacity |
| Version stability | Pin a model and runtime for repeatable releases | Security updates and deliberate model upgrades |
| Low-latency access to private data | Place inference close to the systems it uses | Retrieval latency, model execution time, and network topology |

An API can remain the simpler choice for intermittent demand, models whose weights are unavailable, or teams that do not want to operate inference infrastructure. Business API use also does not automatically mean prompts train the provider's models. For example, OpenAI's API data controls distinguish training use from retention and endpoint-specific behaviour.

## Which models and runtimes can you self-host?

Choose a model with downloadable weights and licence terms that permit your intended use, then select a runtime that supports its architecture and hardware.

Open weights and open source are not interchangeable promises. Check commercial use, redistribution, attribution, and any acceptable-use conditions for the exact model version. A model family name is not enough to establish its licence.

For a small instruction-following example, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 has an Apache 2.0 licence and instructions for serving with vLLM. It is a practical starting point for testing deployment mechanics; it is not a universal recommendation for every production task.

Common runtime choices include:

- vLLM: GPU model serving with an OpenAI-compatible API and controls for memory, batching, and concurrency.
- Ollama: A convenient local model workflow for development and evaluation.
- llama.cpp: Inference across a range of hardware, including quantised models in GGUF format.

Select the runtime after checking the exact model, quantisation format, and accelerator. Support for a model family in one configuration does not establish compatibility with every converted checkpoint.

## How much GPU memory do self-hosted AI models need?

A model needs memory for its weights plus runtime allocations and the working state of active requests. Parameter count alone is not a complete sizing calculation.

A rough weight-only estimate is:

```text
Weight memory in bytes ≈ parameter count × bytes per parameter
```

For four billion parameters at two bytes per parameter, weights alone occupy roughly 8 GB in decimal units. Quantisation can reduce that portion, but it adds format-specific overhead and may affect quality or speed.

Language-model serving also uses memory for the key-value cache, which grows with the request workload. Longer contexts and more concurrent requests can make a configuration run out of memory even when the weights fit comfortably.

The vLLM memory guidance explains controls such as reducing maximum sequence length or concurrency. Use these deliberately: fitting a smaller GPU is not useful if the resulting limits prevent the application from working.

Check system RAM and disk space separately. Loading weights, downloading model files, and preparing inputs can exhaust host resources before GPU memory becomes the bottleneck. Our GPU selection guide covers the hardware comparison in more detail.

## How do you deploy a self-hosted AI model on Northflank?

Deploy a model-serving container, give it suitable GPU and storage resources, protect its endpoint, and test the response from your application. The following example uses Northflank's managed cloud and vLLM to serve Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.

You need a Northflank account with at least $50 in account credit for managed GPU deployment, an available GPU plan, and a local terminal with `curl`. Review the full resource estimate before creating the workload.

### Step 1: Choose a GPU-enabled project and container

Create a project in a GPU-enabled region, then create a deployment service using an external container image.

Use the official vLLM image:

```text
vllm/vllm-openai:latest
```

The managed GPU deployment guide covers the project and resource controls. Start with one service instance and select a GPU plan with enough memory for the model, runtime, and intended concurrency.

For a reproducible production deployment, replace `latest` with the image version or digest that passes your validation. A new image release should go through the same tests as an application change.

### Step 2: Configure the model server

Set the container's custom entrypoint to `vllm` and its command to the following value in Northflank's runtime settings:

```text
serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --max-model-len 4096
```

Together, the entrypoint and command run `vllm serve ...`. These values belong in the service configuration, not y
